title: How to Build a Custom Under-Stair Storage System: Complete Step-by-Step Tutorial for 2026
excerpt: Learn how to build a custom under-stair storage system in 2026. Step-by-step tutorial with tools, materials, and pro tips to maximize every inch.
content: If you have a staircase in your home, you are sitting on one of the most underused **under-stair storage** opportunities in residential design. That triangular cavity beneath your stairs can hold an impressive amount of gear, from seasonal items and shoes to books, sports equipment, and household supplies. The challenge is that most people either leave the space completely empty or throw things in there without any real system. In this complete step-by-step tutorial, I will walk you through exactly how to plan, build, and finish a custom under-stair storage system from scratch in 2026, so you can finally make that dead space work hard for your household.
![Custom built under-stair storage system with pull-out drawers and open shelving in a modern home](/images/blog/how-to-build-custom-under-stair-storage-system-step-by-step-tutorial-2026-hero.webp)
## Why Under-Stair Storage Is One of the Best Home Organization Moves in 2026

The average under-stair cavity in a standard American home measures anywhere from 5 to 10 feet wide and up to 8 feet tall at its highest point. That translates to a serious amount of cubic footage that most households never tap into. According to [The Spruce](https://www.thespruce.com), making use of awkward architectural spaces like under-stair areas is one of the top home organization strategies recommended by professional organizers precisely because it adds real usable storage without requiring a renovation or an addition.
Beyond raw square footage, there are several compelling reasons to build a proper system here rather than leaving the space raw or simply stacking boxes.
• **Reduces visible clutter** throughout the rest of your home by giving frequently-used items a permanent, hidden home
• **Increases your home's perceived value** since built-in storage is considered a desirable feature by buyers
• **Makes daily routines faster** by keeping shoes, bags, and everyday-use items organized and accessible near your entryway
• **Prevents the creep of clutter** into living rooms, bedrooms, and hallways
• **Maximizes your existing footprint** without spending money on an addition or a storage unit rental

If you have been looking at [under staircase storage ideas](/blog/under-staircase-storage-ideas) for inspiration, this tutorial will take those concepts and turn them into an actionable build you can complete over a weekend or two.

## Step 1: Assess Your Under-Stair Space Before You Build Anything

Before you pick up a single tool, you need to understand exactly what you are working with. Every staircase is slightly different, and rushing into cuts without a thorough assessment is the number one mistake DIY builders make on this type of project.
### Measure the Space Accurately
Grab a tape measure and record the following dimensions:
1. **The full width** of the stair cavity from one wall to the other
2. **The height at the tallest point**, which is typically at the base of the highest riser
3. **The height at the shortest point**, which is near the floor at the far end
4. **The depth from front to back**, measured at several intervals because the depth changes as the slope rises
5. **The location of any existing studs**, pipes, or electrical runs inside the wall

Write all of these down and sketch a rough side-view diagram. If your stairs run parallel to a wall, you may have a simple rectangular footprint. If they turn or are freestanding, the geometry gets more complex. Take your time here.
### Identify What You Need to Store
This step sounds obvious but most people skip it and then build something that does not actually serve their needs. Ask yourself:
• What are you currently storing in disorganized piles around the house that you wish had a home?
• Do you need deep pull-out drawers for bulky items, or tall open shelves for bins and baskets?
• Are you planning to store anything tall, like a vacuum cleaner or umbrellas, that needs a dedicated vertical slot?
• Will children access this space, requiring lower shelves and safety hardware?

Your answers will directly shape the configuration you build. For most American households, a combination of pull-out drawers at the base, adjustable shelves in the mid-section, and a tall closet-style section at the highest point works extremely well.
### Check for Obstructions

Use a stud finder to locate any studs, pipes, or wiring inside the cavity wall. If you find electrical wiring, consult a licensed electrician before proceeding. Building around plumbing is possible but requires planning. Structural concerns involving load-bearing walls should always be reviewed by a contractor before you open up the space.
![Woodworking tools laid out on a workbench for a home storage building project](/images/blog/how-to-build-custom-under-stair-storage-system-step-by-step-tutorial-2026-section-tools.webp)
## Step 2: Gather Your Tools and Materials for Under-Stair Storage Construction
One of the great things about this type of project is that it does not require exotic tools or specialty lumber. Most of what you need is available at any home improvement store.
### Tools You Will Need
• **Circular saw or miter saw** for cutting plywood and dimensional lumber to length
• **Drill and driver bits** for pilot holes and driving screws
• **Level** (at least 4 feet long) to ensure shelves and frames are plumb and flat
• **Tape measure and pencil** for marking cuts
• **Stud finder** for locating wall studs
• **Jigsaw** for any curved or notched cuts around obstructions
• **Sandpaper** in 80-grit and 120-grit for finishing edges
• **Paintbrushes and roller** if you plan to paint the finished unit
• **Safety glasses and ear protection**
### Materials Shopping List
For a typical under-stair build covering roughly 6 feet of width, plan on the following:
• **3/4-inch plywood** (sanded or birch face for a cleaner look): 6 to 8 full sheets
• **1x4 and 2x4 dimensional lumber** for the frame and face frame
• **Wood screws** (1-5/8 inch and 2-1/2 inch lengths)
• **Wood glue**
• **Drawer slides** (full-extension, soft-close recommended): one pair per drawer
• **Shelf pins** for adjustable shelves
• **Cabinet hinges** if you are adding doors
• **Cabinet pulls or knobs**
• **Wood filler and sandpaper** for finishing
• **Primer and paint or wood stain** for the final finish

> Budget tip: For a 6-foot under-stair storage build using standard plywood and basic hardware, expect to spend between US$300 and US$700 depending on your material choices and hardware quality. Using paint-grade birch plywood with soft-close drawer slides lands most projects in the middle of that range.

## Step 3: Plan Your Layout and Build the Frame
Now that you have your measurements and materials, it is time to plan the exact layout on paper and then transfer that plan into physical framing inside the space.
### Sketch Your Final Layout
Using your measurements, draw a to-scale front-view layout of the storage unit. Divide the width into sections. A common and highly functional configuration for a 6-foot-wide cavity looks like this:
1. **Left section (24 inches wide):** Tall open area for a vacuum, brooms, or hanging coats, with a rod at the top
2. **Middle section (24 inches wide):** Three to four adjustable shelves for bins, books, or small appliances
3. **Right section (24 inches wide):** Two or three pull-out drawers at the base for shoes, sports gear, or tools
Adjust proportions based on your specific needs. If you have a particularly tall peak point, you might stack drawers four high on one side.
### Build and Install the Base Frame
Start by building a simple rectangular base frame from 2x4 lumber that sits on the floor. This lifts the unit slightly, protects the plywood from moisture, and gives you something solid to anchor to.
1. Cut 2x4s to form a perimeter rectangle matching your planned footprint
2. Add cross members every 24 inches for support
3. Level the frame using shims if your floor is not perfectly flat
4. Secure the frame to the floor using 3-inch screws driven into the subfloor
### Build the Vertical Dividers and Outer Walls

Cut your 3/4-inch plywood panels for the outer walls and internal vertical dividers. The outer walls run from the base frame up to meet the underside of the stair risers. The internal dividers separate your three sections.
• Cut each panel carefully, test-fitting before fastening
• Use wood glue and 1-5/8-inch screws to join panels to the base frame
• Check every panel for plumb (straight up-and-down) using your level before driving the final screws
• Secure tall panels to wall studs using 2-1/2-inch screws for stability
![Wooden stud framing inside an under-stair storage cavity during a DIY build](/images/blog/how-to-build-custom-under-stair-storage-system-step-by-step-tutorial-2026-section-framing.webp)
## Step 4: Install Shelves in Your Under-Stair Storage System
With your frame and dividers in place, adding shelves is one of the most satisfying parts of the build. This is where the space starts to look like real storage.
### Adjustable vs. Fixed Shelves

I strongly recommend making at least some of your shelves adjustable, especially if you are not 100% sure what you will be storing long-term. Adjustable shelves require shelf pin holes drilled in the side panels every inch or two, which takes about 15 minutes with a drill and a simple shelf-pin jig.
Fixed shelves are appropriate for the base of a drawer section where you know the exact height you need.
### Installing Adjustable Shelves
1. Mark a vertical row of shelf-pin holes on both inner faces of each section's side panels
2. Space holes 1 inch apart, starting 3 inches from the top and bottom of the usable space
3. Use a shelf-pin drilling jig to keep holes aligned and consistent
4. Cut shelf panels from 3/4-inch plywood to fit each section with about 1/8-inch clearance on each side
5. Sand all shelf edges smooth before dropping them in
6. Insert shelf pins and rest the shelf on top

> Pro tip: Cut a small notch at the back corners of each shelf panel to allow it to fit flush against the wall even if the baseboard molding runs behind the unit. A 3/4-inch by 3/4-inch notch is usually enough.

![Finished open wooden shelves inside under-stair space holding organized fabric storage bins](/images/blog/how-to-build-custom-under-stair-storage-system-step-by-step-tutorial-2026-section-shelves.webp)
## Step 5: Build and Install Pull-Out Drawers

Pull-out drawers are what really elevate a basic under-stair build into a functional storage system. They let you access items at the back without getting on your hands and knees, and they look polished and intentional.
### Sizing Your Drawers

Each drawer consists of two parts: the **drawer box** (the structural container that holds your items) and the **drawer front** (the decorative face you see when the drawer is closed). Size the drawer box to fit your drawer slides with the clearances specified by the slide manufacturer, typically 1/2 inch on each side.
For a 24-inch wide section with full-extension slides, your drawer box width will be approximately 21 inches. Height is up to you, but 6 to 8 inches is a practical height for shoe and gear storage.
### Building the Drawer Boxes
1. Cut four pieces of 1/2-inch plywood per drawer: two sides, one front, and one back
2. Cut a bottom panel from 1/4-inch plywood
3. Assemble with wood glue and 1-5/8-inch screws, driving screws through the side panels into the front and back pieces
4. Slide the bottom panel into a dado groove or attach it to the bottom edges with glue and brad nails
5. Check the box for square by measuring diagonally corner to corner. Both measurements should be equal.
### Installing the Drawer Slides
1. Mount the fixed half of each slide to the inside of the drawer section's side panels at your marked heights
2. Mount the moving half of each slide to the outside of the drawer box
3. Test fit the drawer box into the opening by snapping the two halves of the slide together
4. Test the action. It should glide smoothly with no binding. Adjust slide height with shims if needed.
### Attaching Drawer Fronts

Cut decorative fronts from 3/4-inch plywood or MDF that overlap the drawer opening by about 1/2 inch on each side and top and bottom. Attach them to the drawer boxes from the inside with screws. Leave a consistent 1/8-inch gap between adjacent fronts for a clean, professional look.

## Step 6: Add Doors, Finishing Touches, and Organization Accessories
This is the step that takes your build from a raw construction project to something that looks like it belongs in a design magazine.
### Installing Cabinet Doors

If you want to close off any section of your under-stair storage, cabinet doors are your best option. Inset doors sit flush inside the opening for a sleek look, while overlay doors cover the opening and are easier for beginners to install and adjust.
1. Cut door panels to your planned size from 3/4-inch plywood or MDF
2. Mount European-style concealed hinges to the inside face of the door
3. Clip the hinges into the mounting plates already screwed to your cabinet frame
4. Adjust the hinge screws for perfect alignment: up-down, left-right, and in-out
5. Attach your chosen pull or knob
### Sanding, Filling, and Painting
A clean finish makes the entire unit look professional and protects the wood.
1. Fill all screw holes and any gaps with wood filler. Allow to dry completely.
2. Sand the entire unit with 80-grit paper, then follow with 120-grit for a smooth surface
3. Wipe down all surfaces with a damp cloth to remove dust
4. Apply a coat of wood primer, allow to dry per the manufacturer's instructions
5. Apply two coats of interior paint in your chosen color, sanding lightly with 220-grit between coats

White or off-white is a popular choice because it brightens the interior of the unit, making it easier to see and access items stored inside. For a warmer look, a soft gray or natural wood stain both photograph beautifully and hold up well in high-traffic areas.
### Add Interior Organization Accessories
Now that the structure is done, it is time to stock it with smart organization products that help you make the most of every inch. I like to use a mix of the following inside under-stair builds:
• **Labeled fabric storage bins** on open shelves for categories like seasonal decor, sports gear, or craft supplies
• **Small clear stackable bins** inside drawers to subdivide space for batteries, chargers, and small tools
• **A tension rod or simple closet rod** in the tall section for hanging bags, umbrellas, or lightweight coats
• **A small LED battery-operated light strip** along the top interior edge, since under-stair cavities often lack natural light
• **Adhesive hooks** on the inside of cabinet doors for keys, leashes, or small tote bags

## Common Mistakes to Avoid When Building Under-Stair Storage
I have helped a number of friends and family members with under-stair builds over the years, and the same mistakes come up again and again. Here is what to watch out for:
• **Skipping the assessment phase:** Building before you measure and identify obstructions leads to expensive re-cuts and wasted materials

• **Not accounting for the slope:** The ceiling of the cavity follows the angle of the stair, so your vertical panels need to be cut at an angle at the top to sit flush. Many first-timers forget this and end up with gaps.
• **Using panels that are too thin:** Always use 3/4-inch plywood for shelves and side panels. Anything thinner will sag over time under the weight of stored items.
• **Ignoring drawer slide clearances:** Every slide manufacturer specifies exact clearances needed. If you ignore these, drawers will bind or fall out.
• **Rushing the finishing:** Raw, unpainted plywood looks unfinished and makes the space feel like a temporary fix. A proper paint or stain job takes a few hours but makes a dramatic difference.
• **Forgetting lighting:** Under-stair cavities are dark. A simple battery-operated LED light strip costs under US$20 and transforms the usability of the space.

## FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions About Under-Stair Storage
**Q: Do I need a building permit to build under-stair storage?**

In most US municipalities, adding built-in storage inside an existing, enclosed under-stair cavity does not require a permit because you are not altering the structure. However, if you plan to open up a wall, add electrical wiring, or cut into a load-bearing element, check with your local building department first. Rules vary by city and county.
**Q: How long does this project take for a beginner?**

A realistic timeline for a beginner working on weekends is two to three weekends. Weekend one covers measuring, planning, and buying materials. Weekend two covers framing, shelving, and drawer installation. Weekend three covers doors, finishing, and painting. Experienced DIYers can often complete the structural work in a single weekend.
**Q: Can I build under-stair storage if my staircase is open (no wall underneath)?**

Yes, but the process is different. Open staircases require you to first frame in the cavity by building walls on one or more sides before you can build the interior storage unit. This adds cost and complexity but is absolutely doable as a DIY project.
**Q: What is the best wood to use for this type of build?**

For painted finishes, I recommend paint-grade birch plywood or MDF for the visible surfaces. For the structural frame and hidden pieces, standard construction plywood or dimensional lumber works perfectly well and costs less.
**Q: How do I handle the sloped ceiling inside the cavity?**

Measure the angle of the slope with a digital angle finder (about US$15 at any hardware store) and use that angle when cutting the tops of your vertical dividers. Alternatively, cut the dividers square and scribe-trim the top edge after installation to fit flush against the sloped underside of the stairs.
**Q: Is this project accessible for someone who has never built furniture before?**

It is at the intermediate DIY level. If you have built basic flat-pack furniture and feel comfortable with a drill, you can do this. The trickiest parts are the angled cuts and getting the drawer slides perfectly aligned. Take your time, dry-fit everything before you fasten it, and watch a few tutorial videos on drawer slide installation before you start.
